params.title: Power Sources
params.subtitle: Cells and batteries, charging safely, how long a battery lasts, and how DC motors and generators behave.

onScreen: Batteries, charging, run time, motors and generators
scenes.narration: Welcome to Power Sources. Every radio needs power, and on a ship that often means batteries for the emergency gear, plus motors and generators that turn electrical power into motion and back again. We'll start with a quick refresher on voltage, current, resistance and power, so you don't need any background. Then we'll look inside a battery cell, see how to charge one safely, and work out how long a battery will run your equipment. Finally, we'll see how DC, or direct current, motors and generators work, why some of them can run away, and how much current a motor draws. By the end, you'll be able to work every calculation in this part of the exam, one step at a time.

onScreen: Voltage E: the push, in volts
Current I: the flow, in amperes
Resistance R: holding back, in ohms
scenes.narration: Let's start with 3 basic quantities, using water in a pipe as our picture. Electricity at work is a flow of electrons, tiny particles that carry an electric charge, around a complete loop called a circuit. Voltage is the electrical push that drives the electrons around the circuit, like water pressure. It's measured in volts, and in formulas it's written E, for electromotive force, or EMF: the force that moves electrons. Current is the flow itself: how many electrons move past a point each second, like the amount of water flowing. It's measured in amperes, or amps, and written I. Resistance is whatever holds the flow back, like a narrow pipe. It's measured in ohms and written R. A battery gives DC, direct current, which flows one way only.

params.title: Ohm's law and power
params.formula: I = E ÷ R and P = E × I
steps: A 6 V battery across a 12 Ω lamp
Power P: how fast energy is used, in watts
params.answer: Turned around: R = E ÷ I and I = P ÷ E

onScreen: Power: P = E × I, in watts
R = E ÷ I and I = P ÷ E
scenes.narration: These quantities are tied together by Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance, I equals E over R. More push means more flow; more resistance means less. Try it on a 6 volt battery connected across a 12 ohm lamp: 6 volts divided by 12 ohms is 0.5 amperes. A fourth quantity, power, is how fast electrical energy is used doing work, such as lighting that lamp. It's measured in watts and written P, and it equals voltage times current, push times flow: P equals E times I. For our lamp, 6 volts times 0.5 amperes is 3 watts. Know any 2 of these quantities and you can find the third by turning the formulas around: R equals E over I, and I equals P over E. We'll use both later.

params.title: Inside a battery: the cell
items: A cell: 2 different plates in a chemical called the electrolyte
The chemical reaction moves electrons from one plate to the other: a voltage
Each plate connects to a terminal: negative or positive
Lead-acid: lead plates in sulfuric acid; rechargeable, so a storage cell
Fully charged lead-acid cell: 2.06 volts on average

onScreen: Lead-acid: lead plates in sulfuric acid
scenes.narration: So where does a battery's push come from? Inside a battery are one or more cells. A cell is 2 different materials, called plates, sitting in a chemical called the electrolyte. The chemical reaction pulls electrons off one plate and piles them onto the other, and that imbalance makes a voltage. Each plate connects to a terminal, a connection post: the negative terminal, with the extra electrons, and the positive terminal. In a lead-acid cell, the kind in a car battery, the plates are lead and lead compounds, in sulfuric acid mixed with water. It can be recharged, so it's called a storage cell. How much push does one cell give? The average fully-charged voltage of a lead-acid storage cell is 2.06 volts.

callouts.label: Series: the + of one cell joined to the − of the next
A single path: the same current flows through every cell
6 cells: a little over 12 volts, called a 12-volt battery

onScreen: Series: + of one to − of the next
scenes.narration: A single cell gives only a small push, so a battery joins several cells in series. Series means one after another: the positive terminal of one cell is joined to the negative terminal of the next, so the current has a single path through them all. In series, voltages add, like stacking steps: each cell lifts the push a little higher. Each lead-acid cell gives 2.06 volts, so 6 of them in series give a little over 12 volts. That's why a 6-cell lead-acid battery is called a 12-volt battery.

params.title: Cell voltages side by side
rows: A trap on the nickel-cadmium question

scenes.narration: Different chemistry gives a different voltage per cell. You've met lead-acid: 2.06 volts when fully charged. The exam's traps are 1, 1.2 and 1.56 volts, and watch 1.2 especially: it's close to the next cell we'll meet, not lead-acid. A nickel-cadmium cell is a rechargeable type. Its operating voltage, the voltage it holds for most of the time it's in use, is about 1.25 volts. That's a little below the 1.5 volts of a fresh alkaline or carbon-zinc cell, the ordinary throwaway kind in a flashlight. On the nickel-cadmium question, the traps are 1.4, 1.5 and 2.1 volts: 1.5 is the alkaline cell, and 2.1 is close to lead-acid.

params.title: Cells in series: 12 nickel-cadmium cells
params.formula: Series total = cells × volts per cell

onScreen: Series total = cells × volts per cell
scenes.narration: Now put the series rule to work. The exam asks for the total voltage of 12 nickel-cadmium batteries connected in series. Here, battery means a single cell; people often use the word loosely. In series the voltages add, so the total is the number of cells times the voltage of each. Each nickel-cadmium cell gives about 1.25 volts, which is 1 and a quarter. So 12 cells give 12 ones, which is 12, plus 12 quarters, which make 3 more: 15 volts in all. The traps: 12 volts assumes 1 volt per cell, 12.6 volts is a common lead-acid battery rating, and 72 volts is far too high.

blocks.label: Charger: a higher voltage
blocks.note: Pushes current in, opposite to normal

onScreen: Charger pushes current in, the opposite way
Chemistry runs backward: energy stored again
scenes.narration: Those are the voltages of charged cells. As a battery is used, its chemicals are used up, and it runs down. A storage battery can be filled up again by charging. A charger is connected to the battery's terminals, positive to positive, and it has a higher voltage than the battery's own. Its stronger push wins, so it drives current into the battery, the opposite way to normal. That makes the chemical reaction run backward, turning the used-up chemicals back into charged ones and storing energy again. That's very useful, but charging a lead-acid battery has a side effect you must know about.

callouts.label: Electrolyte: sulfuric acid mixed with water
Near full charge, the current splits the water
Hydrogen gas escapes from the vents
Hydrogen is explosive in air: one spark can set it off
Charge in a well-ventilated space, away from sparks and flames

scenes.narration: Here's the side effect, and it's harmful to people. Remember that the electrolyte is sulfuric acid mixed with water, and water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Near full charge, the current has little chemistry left to reverse, so it splits the water instead, and hydrogen gas escapes from the vents. Hydrogen is explosive in air: a single spark can set it off. So always charge in a well-ventilated space, away from sparks and flames. Some oxygen comes off too, but the danger is hydrogen. Chlorine is a trap, since this battery makes none, and so is plate sulfation, a crust that harms the battery, not you.

params.title: Trickle charging from a 110 V DC line

scenes.narration: Charging safely also means controlling the current, and the exam has a problem on exactly that. Trickle charging means charging slowly, with a small, steady current. The exam's battery has a terminal voltage of 12.5 volts, the voltage across its terminals. It's to be trickle-charged at 0.5 amperes from a 110 volt DC supply line. Connected straight to the line, far too much current would rush in, because the extra push would meet almost no resistance. So we add a resistor, a part made to have a set resistance, in series with the battery. The battery pushes back with its own 12.5 volts, so the resistor must drop, or use up, the rest: 110 minus 12.5, which is 97.5 volts. The same 0.5 amperes flows through both, because in series there's only one path.

params.title: The series charging resistor
steps: Voltage to drop: 110 V − 12.5 V = 97.5 V

scenes.narration: Now find the resistor with Ohm's law turned around: R equals E over I. Here E is the voltage the resistor must drop, the line voltage minus the battery voltage, and I is the charging current. Step 1: 110 volts minus 12.5 volts is 97.5 volts. Step 2: the current is 0.5 amperes. Step 3: 97.5 volts divided by 0.5 amperes. Dividing by a half is the same as doubling, so that's 195 ohms. Check it: 97.5 volts across 195 ohms drives exactly 0.5 amperes. The trap 95 ohms would let about 1 ampere through, twice the rate, and 300 ohms would charge too slowly.

Charging fills a battery up. So how much can it hold? That's its capacity, measured in ampere-hours: 1 ampere-hour means 1 ampere flowing for 1 hour. Take a 50 ampere-hour battery. In the simple arithmetic the exam uses, it can supply 1 ampere for 50 hours, since 1 times 50 is 50. It can also supply 5 amperes for 10 hours, since 5 times 10 is also 50. Think of a water tank: capacity is how much it holds, and current is how fast you drain it. Drain it faster and it empties sooner: at 50 amperes, it lasts just 1 hour. So battery capacity in ampere-hours equals load current times time, where the load is whatever the battery powers.

params.title: Sizing a battery: ampere-hours needed
steps: Given: 70% of 40 A, plus a 1.5 A light, for 6 h

onScreen: 70% of 40 A, a 1.5 A light, 6 hours
scenes.narration: Now use that rule to size a battery for a job. A transmitter must run for 6 hours on a storage battery. Its key-locked demand, the current it draws with its transmit key locked down, is 40 amperes. It doesn't transmit nonstop, so its continuous load is 70 percent of that. An emergency light adds 1.5 amperes. First, the total current. 70 percent is 0.7, so the transmitter draws 0.7 times 40 amperes; 10 percent of 40 is 4, so that's 7 times 4. Add the light's 1.5 amperes, for a total of 29.5 amperes. Then the capacity: current times time, so 29.5 amperes times 6 hours is 177 ampere-hours. The question also calls it a 50 watt transmitter; you don't need that number. Forget the 70 percent, and you land on the trap, 249.

params.title: How long will the battery last?

blocks.label: 1. Add the watts of all loads

scenes.narration: So that's how big a battery a job needs. The next set of questions turns it around: you already have a battery, so how long will it run your equipment? Step 1: add the power of all the loads, because they all run from the battery at once. Equipment is rated in watts, meaning its label says how much power it uses, but the battery is rated in ampere-hours, so we need a bridge between them, and that bridge is current. Step 2: find the current with I equals P over E, using the battery's voltage for E. Step 3: divide the battery's ampere-hour rating by that current. Ampere-hours divided by amperes leaves hours, so the answer is the run time.

Let's work the first exam example. An emergency transmitter uses 325 watts and a receiver uses 50 watts. How many hours can a 12.6 volt, 55 ampere-hour battery supply full power to both? Step 1, total power: 325 plus 50 is 375 watts. Step 2, current: 375 watts divided by 12.6 volts is about 29.8 amperes. Step 3, time: 55 ampere-hours divided by 29.8 amperes is about 1.85 hours, which the exam lists as 1.8 hours. Is that reasonable? 29.8 amperes is a bit more than half of 55, so the battery should last a bit under 2 hours, and it does.

params.title: Run time in hours and minutes
steps: Part of an hour × 60 → about 43 minutes

scenes.narration: Same 3 steps, with 1 extra step at the end. A ship's radar, the set that spots other ships and land on a screen, uses 315 watts and a radio uses 50 watts, on a 50 ampere-hour battery rated at 12.6 volts. Total power: 315 plus 50 is 365 watts. Current: 365 divided by 12.6 is about 28.97 amperes. Time: 50 ampere-hours divided by 28.97 amperes is about 1.73 hours. The answers here are in hours and minutes, so convert: 1.73 hours is 1 whole hour plus part of an hour. Multiply that part by 60 minutes, and you get a little over 43 minutes. So the battery lasts about 1 hour 43 minutes, the exam's answer.

params.title: Run time on a 12 volt battery

scenes.narration: Next, a marine radiotelephone, a ship's two-way voice radio: its receiver uses 75 watts and its transmitter uses 325 watts. How long can both run before they discharge, or run down, a 50 ampere-hour, 12 volt battery? This battery is 12 volts, not 12.6, so use 12. Total power: 75 plus 325 is 400 watts. Current: 400 divided by 12 is about 33.3 amperes. Time: 50 ampere-hours divided by 33.3 amperes is 1.5 hours, which the exam writes as 1 and a half hours. Check it backward: 1.5 hours times 33.3 amperes is about 50 ampere-hours.

params.title: Run time on a small battery

scenes.narration: Last one, with a much smaller battery. A 12.6 volt, 8 ampere-hour battery runs a 50 watt receiver and a 300 watt radar. Total power: 50 plus 300 is 350 watts. Current: 350 divided by 12.6 is about 27.8 amperes. Time: 8 ampere-hours divided by 27.8 amperes is about 0.29 hours, less than a third of an hour. To get minutes, multiply by 60: about 17 minutes. Rounded, that's 0.3 hours, so the exam lists 17 minutes or 0.3 hours. It makes sense: a small 8 ampere-hour battery can't feed 27.8 amperes for long.

Here are the 4 problems side by side, all solved the same way: watts to amperes, then ampere-hours divided by amperes. 375 watts on a 55 ampere-hour battery draws about 29.8 amperes and lasts about 1.8 hours. 365 watts on 50 ampere-hours draws 28.97 amperes and lasts 1 hour 43 minutes. The trap 28.97 hours is really the current, in amperes, not a time. 400 watts on 50 ampere-hours draws 33.3 amperes and lasts 1 and a half hours. This battery is 12 volts, not 12.6, which is why the current is higher. And 350 watts on just 8 ampere-hours lasts only 17 minutes. Its traps, 27.7 and 100.8 hours, aren't times either: 100.8 is volts times ampere-hours, which gives watt-hours, a measure of stored energy.

params.title: A real battery has resistance inside

onScreen: Load resistance: the lamp or radio
Same current through both: in series
scenes.narration: So far we've treated a battery as a perfect source of push. A real battery also has a small resistance inside it: its plates, its electrolyte and its connections all hold the current back a little. That's its internal resistance. The current passes through it on every trip around the circuit, so it sits in series with the load. In series, resistances simply add, like 2 narrow sections of the same pipe. So the current equals the battery voltage divided by the load resistance plus the internal resistance. The extra resistance always means a little less current than the load alone would draw.

onScreen: 6 V ÷ 12.01 Ω ≈ 0.4996 A, listed as 0.4995 amps
scenes.narration: Here's the exam's version. A 6 volt storage battery has an internal resistance of 0.01 ohms, and a 3-watt, 6-volt lamp is connected. What current flows? First, the lamp's resistance. The shortcut is R equals E squared over P. E squared means E times itself, so 6 times 6, divided by 3 watts, gives 12 ohms. The 2 formulas from the start agree: 3 watts at 6 volts is 0.5 amperes, and 6 volts over 0.5 amperes is 12 ohms. Next, add the internal resistance: 12 plus 0.01 is 12.01 ohms. Finally, 6 volts divided by 12.01 ohms is about 0.4996 amperes, which the exam lists as 0.4995 amps. Just under 0.5 makes sense: the tiny internal resistance trims the current slightly, so the answers above 0.5 can't be right.

params.title: Series and parallel
rows: One after another: a single path
Side by side: a separate path each
Less than any one of them

onScreen: Two 12 Ω bulbs in parallel = 6 Ω
scenes.narration: The second internal-resistance problem uses a parallel load, so let's compare the 2 ways to connect parts. You know series: parts one after another, a single path, so their resistances add. In parallel, parts sit side by side, each across the same voltage, and each gives the current its own path. More paths let more current through, just like opening a second pipe beside the first, so the total resistance goes down. For 2 equal resistances in parallel, the total is exactly half of one. So 2 bulbs of 12 ohms each, in parallel, act like 6 ohms.

params.title: Internal resistance: two bulbs in parallel
steps: Two 12 Ω bulbs in parallel = 6 Ω
Add the internal resistance: 6 Ω + 1.2 Ω = 7.2 Ω

onScreen: Two 12 Ω bulbs in parallel = 6 Ω
scenes.narration: Now the full problem. A 6 volt battery with 1.2 ohms of internal resistance is connected across 2 light bulbs in parallel, 12 ohms each. Step 1: the bulbs together make 6 ohms. Step 2: the internal resistance is in series with that pair, so add it: 6 plus 1.2 is 7.2 ohms. Step 3: I equals E over R, 6 volts divided by 7.2 ohms, which is about 0.83 amperes. Compare that with no internal resistance at all: 6 volts across 6 ohms would give 1 ampere, which is the trap 1.0 amps. The internal resistance holds the current down to 0.83.

params.title: From current to motion: the DC motor
items: Motor: electrical power into motion. Generator: motion into electrical power
Current through a coil makes a magnetic field: an electromagnet
Opposite poles attract; like poles repel
Field winding: a fixed electromagnet. Armature: the coil that spins inside it
Brushes: sliding contacts that feed current to the armature

onScreen: Opposite poles attract, like poles repel
Brushes feed current to the armature
scenes.narration: That's the battery side of the lesson. Now for the machines: a motor turns electrical power into motion, and a generator turns motion into electrical power. Both rest on magnetism. Whenever current flows through a wire, it makes a magnetic field around it, and winding the wire into a coil around iron makes a strong one: an electromagnet. Every magnet has 2 ends, called its north and south poles: opposite poles attract, and like poles repel. In a DC motor, a fixed electromagnet, made by a coil called the field winding, surrounds a second coil that can turn, called the armature. Brushes, sliding contacts, feed current into the armature, making it a magnet too. The field pushes and pulls on it, and the armature turns.

params.title: A generator: a motor run backward

blocks.label: Through the field's flux
blocks.note: Flux: the magnetism through the coil

blocks.label: Voltage induced in the coil
blocks.note: Faster spin or more flux: more volts

blocks.label: AC, or DC via a commutator

onScreen: Voltage is induced: more speed or flux, more voltage
AC, or DC with a commutator
scenes.narration: Run the idea backward and you get a generator. Use an engine to spin the armature, so its coil sweeps through the field's magnetism. The amount of magnetism passing through the coil is called the magnetic flux. As the coil moves through the flux, a voltage is induced, or created, in it. The faster the coil spins, and the more flux there is, the more voltage you get. Remember this: the voltage depends on speed and flux. A spinning coil naturally makes a voltage that swings back and forth every turn: AC, alternating current. A DC generator adds a rotating switch, called a commutator, to send its output out one way.

params.title: Counter-EMF: every motor is a generator

blocks.label: Current falls
blocks.note: Only supply minus counter-EMF drives it

onScreen: Supply drives current; the armature spins
Current falls as the speed rises
scenes.narration: Now put the motor and the generator together. The supply pushes current through the armature, and the armature spins. But a spinning armature is a coil moving through a magnetic field, so it's a generator too. It makes its own voltage, which pushes back against the supply: counter-EMF, or counter electromotive force. Only the difference between the supply voltage and the counter-EMF drives current through the armature, and that current makes the turning force. So as the motor speeds up, its counter-EMF grows and the current falls, until the speed settles, with the counter-EMF nearly equal to the supply. Now the twist: if the field gets weaker, each turn makes less counter-EMF, so the motor must spin faster before it settles. Weaker field, higher speed.

params.title: Series motor with its load removed

blocks.label: Series motor: load removed
blocks.note: Field and armature share one current

onScreen: Series motor: field in series with the armature
scenes.narration: Keep that rule in mind for the 2 kinds of DC motor the exam asks about. In a series motor, the field winding is connected in series with the armature, so the same current flows through both. Remove the load from an operating series motor, and with nothing to turn, it speeds up, its counter-EMF rises, and little current flows. But that small current is also the field current, so the field weakens, and with a weaker field the motor must spin ever faster to generate counter-EMF. It's a runaway loop, and nothing holds it back: it will accelerate until it falls apart. That's why series motors are kept coupled to their loads. The traps, that it stops, speeds up slightly, or doesn't change, all miss this runaway.

params.title: Shunt motor with its field opened
items: Shunt: a side path. The field winding is in parallel, across the supply
Its own steady field current: a fairly steady speed
Shunt field opened: no field current, only weak residual magnetism
Weak field: it must spin much faster to make counter-EMF
So it speeds up, possibly to a dangerous runaway

onScreen: Shunt motor: field across the supply
scenes.narration: A shunt motor is wired differently. Shunt means a side path: its field winding is connected in parallel, straight across the supply. So the field gets its own steady current, whatever the load, and the motor holds a fairly steady speed. But suppose a shunt motor is running with a load and its shunt field is opened, meaning the field's circuit is broken. No field current flows. All that's left is residual magnetism, the weak magnetism that stays in the iron. With such a weak field, the motor must spin much faster to make enough counter-EMF. So it will speed up, possibly to a dangerous runaway. It won't slow down, stop or stay unaffected, as the traps say. In both motors, a weaker field means a faster motor.

params.title: A shunt-wound generator under load
rows: Current loses volts in the windings
The most current it's built to supply

onScreen: No load: voltage at its highest
Load current loses volts in the windings
Full load: voltage at its lowest
scenes.narration: Generators have exam questions of their own: how steady their voltage is, and how to control it. Start with a shunt-wound DC generator: its field winding is connected across its own output, like the shunt motor's field across its supply. With no load, meaning nothing connected, no current flows out, and the voltage is at its highest. Now connect a load. Current flows, and it loses some voltage in the generator's own windings, much like a battery's internal resistance, so the output voltage starts to sag. The more current, the bigger the sag. At full load, the most current the generator is built to supply, the voltage is at its lowest.

params.title: Generator voltage regulation
steps: NL: no load. FL: full load.
Example: 110 V at no load, 100 V at full load
params.answer: Voltage change from load to no-load

onScreen: Voltage regulation: change from load to no-load
No-load minus full-load, as a percentage of full-load
scenes.narration: How much it sags is described by the generator's voltage regulation. For a shunt-wound DC generator, the expression voltage regulation refers to the voltage fluctuations from load to no-load. It's usually given as the no-load voltage minus the full-load voltage, as a percentage of the full-load voltage. Say a generator gives 110 volts at no load and 100 at full load. It changes by 10 volts, and 10 out of 100 is 10 percent. A smaller figure means a steadier voltage. The traps call it output efficiency, or a ratio between 2 windings; it's neither. It's simply how much the output moves as the load comes and goes.

blocks.label: Output voltage
blocks.note: At constant speed, set by the flux

onScreen: Field current from a separate source
Output controlled by the amount of field current
scenes.narration: That's how steady a generator is. Now, how do you control its output? Excited means supplied with field current. In a separately-excited AC generator, the field current comes not from the generator's own output but from a separate source, often called the exciter. That source drives the field current, and you can adjust it. The field current sets the magnetic flux. Remember, the voltage depends on speed and flux. At a constant speed, the only thing left to change is the flux, and the output voltage is proportional to it: double the flux, and you double the voltage. So the output is controlled by the amount of field current. Not the armature or the brushes, and not the exciter itself, which is only the source.

params.title: How motors and generators react
rows: Voltage regulation: how much it changes

onScreen: Series motor, load removed: falls apart
Shunt motor, field opened: speeds up
Generator voltage regulation: load to no-load
Separately-excited generator: field current sets output
scenes.narration: Before moving on, let's line up the 4 machine facts. A series DC motor with its load removed accelerates until it falls apart, because its field weakens along with the current. A shunt motor with its shunt field opened speeds up, possibly to a runaway, because only residual magnetism is left. For a shunt-wound DC generator, voltage regulation means the voltage fluctuations from load to no-load. And the output of a separately-excited AC generator at constant speed is controlled by the amount of field current.

blocks.label: Input = output ÷ efficiency
blocks.note: Efficiency: the share that becomes work

onScreen: DC motor: I = input watts ÷ E
scenes.narration: Back to motors for the last skill: working out how much current one draws. Start with horsepower, a unit of mechanical power still used for motors: 1 horsepower is about 746 watts, or more exactly 745.7. So a motor's output in watts is its horsepower times 746. But no motor is perfect. Its efficiency is the share of the electrical power going in that comes out as useful work; the rest becomes heat. So the input is always more than the output: input watts equal output divided by efficiency. Finally, the current of a DC motor is I equals P over E, using the input watts for P, because that's what the supply has to deliver.

Try it on the exam's DC example. A 3 horsepower, 100 volt DC motor is 85 percent efficient when developing its rated output, the full power it's designed for. What's the current? Step 1, output: 3 times 746 is 2,238 watts. Step 2, input: 85 percent is 0.85, and 2,238 divided by 0.85 is about 2,633 watts, a little more than the output, as it should be. Step 3, current: 2,633 watts divided by 100 volts is about 26.3 amperes, listed on the exam as 26.300 amps.

params.title: AC motors: the power factor
items: AC: voltage and current swing back and forth
In an AC motor, the current swings a little out of step with the voltage
So it draws extra current for the same power
Power factor, PF: a number up to 1 that accounts for this
AC motor current: I = P ÷ (E × PF)

onScreen: Current out of step with voltage
Extra current for the same power
scenes.narration: That's a DC motor. An AC motor needs 1 more step. Remember that AC swings back and forth. In an AC motor, the current swings too, but a little out of step with the voltage, so part of the current does no useful work. The motor has to draw extra current for the same power. The power factor, PF, is a number up to 1 that accounts for this: the further out of step, the smaller it is. So for an AC motor, I equals P over the quantity E times PF. Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger: more current, just as we said.

params.title: Line current of an AC motor

scenes.narration: Now the exam's AC example. It asks for line current: the current the motor draws from its supply line. What's the line current of a 7 horsepower motor on 120 volts at full load, with a power factor of 0.8, and 95 percent efficient? Step 1, output: this one uses the exact figure, so 7 times 745.7 watts is about 5,220 watts. Step 2, input: 5,220 divided by 0.95 is about 5,495 watts. Step 3, current: multiply 120 volts by the power factor, 0.8, which gives just under 100. Then divide 5,495 watts by that, and you get about 57.2 amperes. Is that reasonable? This motor is more than twice as powerful as the DC one, so roughly twice the current makes sense.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Lead-acid cell: 2.06 V; nickel-cadmium: about 1.25 V; in series, voltages add
Charging releases hydrogen, explosive in air: ventilate, no sparks or flames
Run time = ampere-hours ÷ (watts ÷ volts); internal resistance adds in series
Weaker field, faster motor; field current sets a generator's output
Motor current: hp × 746, ÷ efficiency, ÷ volts, and ÷ power factor for AC

onScreen: Run time; internal resistance in series
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up with the 5 things to remember. A lead-acid cell gives 2.06 volts and a nickel-cadmium cell about 1.25, and cells in series add their voltages. Charging a lead-acid battery releases hydrogen, which is explosive in air, so ventilate and keep sparks and flames away. For run time, add up the watts and divide by the volts to get amperes, then divide the ampere-hours by the amperes, and remember that internal resistance adds in series with the load. Weaken a motor's field and it speeds up, sometimes until it falls apart, while a generator's output at constant speed is set by its field current. And for motor current: horsepower times 746, divided by the efficiency, then by the volts, and for AC by the power factor too. Well done.
